sentences.text: The snow came on the night of the twenty-second, which was nine days after the hare turned, and it did not stop for four days.
It was not a normal fall.
That has to be said, because otherwise the story sounds smug and it was not smug at the time; it was frightening.

Two metres came down onto ground that was not frozen, which meant the whole lot sat there wet and enormously heavy, and the power went at some point on the second night, and the road out was not cleared until the twenty-eighth.
Nobody was hurt.
Marit wants that first.
Nobody in Bjørnstad was hurt, that year or any year, and the village is still there and so is most of what happened to it.
But the Hansens lost their long greenhouse, which went in under the weight on the second night with a noise she heard from her bedroom.
Four houses at the top lost water for fourteen days because the pump was not boarded.
The Iversens' potatoes were still in the ground and stayed in the ground and came up in April as a smell.

And on the third morning, in a whiteout, with the power off, Kristian from the garage went out on the tractor and got as far as the top houses, because his tractor had a blade on it, because he had put the blade on it on the fourteenth of October when the forecast said mild.
Marit's father did not say anything about the hare that winter.

He did not admit anything either — that is not how he was made — and the two of them never had a conversation where he said *you were right* or *the hare was right*, because that was not available in that house.
What he did was this.

The following autumn, on the morning the hare turned, which that year was the fourth of November and entirely reasonable, Marit came downstairs at half past six and her father was already dressed and had the box of potato sacks out on the table.
He said, "It's turned, then." And she said, "Yes." And he said, "Right," and went out.
She has thought about that a great deal since, because she works in meteorology now, which several people in the village find extremely funny.
She has run the numbers on it.

She has the records — the parish kept the date of the turning and the date of the first snow going back to 1911, in a ledger, because of course they did — and she has done the arithmetic properly, with error bars, twice, as an adult who is paid to do exactly this.
The gap is seven days, plus or minus two, for a hundred and fourteen years.
She has no explanation.
There are three or four candidates and none of them survives contact with the data, and she has written about it once, carefully, in a journal that six people read.
What she says, when people ask her at conferences, is that she does not know how the hare does it and that this has never once been the interesting part.

The interesting part is that her village had a hundred and fourteen years of a signal that worked, and a mild October, and a forecast on a phone, and that half of them looked at all three of those things and picked the one that came with an explanation.
